what_its_for: Iloperidone is used to treat schizophrenia in adults. Schizophrenia is a mental health condition that can cause symptoms like hearing or seeing things that are not there (hallucinations), believing things that are not true (delusions), and confused thinking. This medicine helps reduce these symptoms so you can feel better and function more in daily life.
how_to_take: Take iloperidone by mouth with or without food. Swallow the tablet whole. Try to take it at the same times each day to help you remember. Do not crush, chew, or split the tablets unless your doctor or pharmacist says it is okay. It is very important NOT to stop taking this medicine suddenly without talking to your doctor first, as this can make your symptoms come back.
dosing: Your doctor will start you on a LOW dose and slowly increase it over the first few days or weeks. This is done on purpose to lower the risk of a sudden drop in blood pressure (which can make you feel dizzy or faint). A typical starting dose is 1 mg twice a day. Your doctor will adjust your dose gradually, usually up to a target dose between 6 mg and 12 mg twice a day, depending on how you respond. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions — do not change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — UNLESS it is almost time for your next dose. In that case, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular scheduled time. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you miss doses for 3 or more days in a row, call your doctor before restarting, because your dose may need to be restarted from a lower amount.
storage: Store iloperidone tablets at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct sunlight. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep this medicine out of the reach of children and pets. Do not use it past the expiration date printed on the package.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking iloperidone, as it can increase dizziness and drowsiness. Avoid driving, operating heavy machinery, or doing activities that need you to be alert until you know how this medicine affects you. Avoid getting up too quickly from a sitting or lying position, as this medicine can cause dizziness and increase your risk of falling. Avoid getting overheated or dehydrated — stay cool and drink enough fluids, especially in hot weather. Avoid taking other medicines that can affect heart rhythm (such as certain antibiotics or heart medicines) without asking your doctor or pharmacist first.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the nearest emergency room if you experience: a fast, pounding, or irregular heartbeat; fainting or feeling like you might faint; high fever, stiff muscles, or confusion (these could be signs of a rare but serious condition called Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome); uncontrollable movements of your face, tongue, or body (this could be a condition called tardive dyskinesia); thoughts of hurting yourself or others; severe dizziness when standing up; signs of high blood sugar such as increased thirst, frequent urination, or blurred vision; or any new or worsening symptoms that concern you.
when_it_works: Iloperidone does not work right away. Most people begin to notice some improvement in symptoms within 1 to 2 weeks, but it may take 4 to 6 weeks or longer to feel the full benefit of this medicine. It is very important to keep taking it every day even if you do not feel better right away. Do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor.
special_populations: Older adults (especially those with dementia): This medicine is NOT approved for treating behavior problems in older adults with dementia and may increase the risk of serious side effects, including death. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Babies born to mothers who take antipsychotic medicines in the last trimester of pregnancy may have temporary withdrawal symptoms or muscle problems after birth. People with liver problems may need a lower dose. People with a history of heart rhythm problems (such as a prolonged QT interval) should use this medicine with caution and tell their doctor about all medicines they take. Always tell your doctor and pharmacist about all prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take.
